name:
Per-person Gmail drafts (

-gmail-drafts MCP)
description: Happy writes drafts into the owner's own Gmail Drafts folder; the owner reviews and sends from Gmail, and Happy has no way to send.
how: `gog --gmail-no-send mcp --allow-write --allow-tool gmail_create_draft,gmail_update_draft`; fail-closed `before_tool_call` block on any send tool; CLI drafts thread with `--reply-to-message-id`.
corrections: The catalog says 'verify `--reply-to-message-id` on drafts create, else drafts are unthreaded'. The upstream command reference documents `--reply-to-message-id` and `--thread-id` on `gog gmail drafts create`, plus a separate `gog gmail drafts reply <messageId>`; the installed SKILL.md (line 59) merely omits them.

The catalog describes a custom MCP around `gog gmail drafts create` with the hook as the only send barrier. Upstream gog's own MCP server already keeps `gmail_send_message` and `gmail_send_draft` behind a separate `--allow-gmail-send` flag, so the hook is a second layer, not the only one.
unverified: Whether gog's MCP tool `gmail_create_draft` exposes the reply and thread parameters that the CLI command has; if not, threaded drafts need a thin wrapper over the CLI.
gog is not installed here; confirm the tool names with `gog mcp --allow-write --list-tools` after install.
The promptfoo 'send attempt is blocked' test is in-house.

name: Lost or stolen phone: lock one person out
description: If a parent's iPhone is lost or stolen, the other parent can stop Happy answering that person's handle with one text, before anyone reaches the Mac. Today the only switch is Tony editing the family file and redeploying.
example: Tony texts: 'Happy, lock out Jordan' after her phone is left in a taxi.
how: Happy trusts the sender's Apple handle: channels.imessage.dmPolicy is 'allowlist' and channels.imessage.allowFrom lists the family, and the same list decides who may answer /approve. Whoever holds an unlocked phone is that person to Happy. The built-in '/allowlist remove' needs commands.config: true, which this install keeps off. So: (1) Today, operator path: remove the handle in family.json5, run gen-family and the deploy script. The docs' incident steps offer the blunt version, dmPolicy 'disabled' for everyone. (2) Build, chat path: extend the kill-switch plugin (G005). A before_dispatch claim matches one exact phrase from an adult's handle, writes the named person's handles to a suspended file, and from then on claims every inbound message from those handles with no reply; the message_sending hook cancels scheduled texts to them. Lifting the suspension is CLI-only. (3) If that phone also ran the OpenClaw app, 'openclaw devices revoke' and 'openclaw devices remove' retire its Gateway token. (4) Phone side, done by the owner from another device: Find My's lost mode locks the phone with its passcode. Enforcement note from review: before_dispatch is a claim hook, and the hook runner's default for claim hooks is to log and continue when a handler throws, while a failed message_sending handler is skipped. A suspension that lives only in those two hooks therefore fails open. The suspended file must also be checked in before_agent_run, which blocks the run before the model reads the prompt, fails closed and carries ctx.senderId, and in before_tool_call for that person's agent. The phrase match itself can stay in before_dispatch.
depends_on: G005 kill-switch plugin (shares the before_dispatch hook)
caveats: A locked phone already stops most of this. The gap is a phone taken while unlocked, or a passcode seen over a shoulder: Apple's Stolen Device Protection page lists the actions it protects and Messages is not among them.
Either adult can lock the other out. That is a nuisance at worst and Tony undoes it at the Mac.
If whoever holds the phone sends the phrase first, the real owner needs the CLI.
After the phone is replaced the handle is the same, so the suspension has to be lifted by hand.
It stops delivery to that person, not their scheduled jobs; pair with pause (G002) if the jobs should stop too.

Apple's Stolen Device Protection page lists opening a locked app among the actions that need Face ID or Touch ID with no passcode fallback. If each parent can lock the Messages app that way, the unlocked-phone gap narrows on the phone itself, with nothing to build (not confirmed, see unverified).
The lock phrase works as a weak shared secret: a thief has to know Happy exists and what the phrase is. Keep it out of Happy's own help text and replies.
safety: The phrase can only narrow access. Nothing in the chat path can add a sender; that stays a reviewed change to family.json5. The chat-path suspension does not take the handle off channels.imessage.allowFrom, which is also the approver list for /approve and for tapback approvals, and the docs say those shortcuts bypass dmPolicy. So only the operator path (remove the handle and redeploy) removes a stolen phone's approver rights. Until that is done, the suspension has to block that person's agent runs and tool calls with fail-closed hooks so that no new approval prompt is raised for the stolen phone to answer, and that person's scheduled jobs should be paused (G002).
unverified: Whether iMessage for a phone number can be re-registered on another device after a SIM swap without the Apple Account password.
Whether owner-only slash commands from a suspended handle are parsed before the before_dispatch hook runs.
Whether the Messages app can be locked with Face ID on the parents' iPhones; Apple's app-lock guide page did not render its body in this run.
What the sender sees when before_agent_run blocks a run and no replacement message is set.
Whether a tapback from a suspended handle can still resolve a pending approval; the docs say reaction approvals bypass dmPolicy and are gated only by the approver list.

name: Guest tier: a grandparent or sitter can text Happy and gets a fridge-level card only
description: A third kind of user between 'family adult' and 'nobody'. A grandparent minding the kids, or a regular sitter, can text Happy and get answers from a short fixed card (bedtimes, allergies, where things are, who to call) and nothing else. Today such a sender is dropped, or if allowlisted lands in the tool-less inbox agent that knows nothing.
example: Grandma texts in Chinese: 'What time does the younger one go to bed, and can she have peanuts?'
how: family.json5 gains a role 'guest'. gen-family adds the guest's handle to channels.imessage.allowFrom and emits a bindings[] entry with match.peer (kind 'direct', id the handle) to a shared 'guest' agent: no tools, memory off, minimal profile, its own workspace whose AGENTS.md is the card, rendered from the sitter facts (F036). Bindings only route; admission is still the allowlist. Replies follow the guest's language (G011). 'Tell the parents ...' is claimed by a before_dispatch pattern and forwarded word for word through the pinned family delivery (G009), the same shape as the kid check-in relay (G018). A dated guest, such as a sitter for one evening, carries an expiry date in the registry; the guest plugin refuses that handle after the date in before_agent_run, which fails closed, and Tony removes the entry at the next reviewed deploy. No unattended job edits the registry or deploys. Whether grandparents also become recipients for G009 is a separate decision; the default stays no, with a parent forwarding drafts. Before the first guest is admitted, set commands.allowFrom to the two parents: it is unset on this install, so command authorization follows the channel allowlist and a guest on allowFrom could send slash commands and inline directives to the guest agent.
depends_on: decision: who beyond the two parents may text Happy
every approval hook checks that the requester is a parent
commands.allowFrom set to the two parents before any guest is admitted
approvals stay in 'session' mode, so an approval id only ever appears in the chat that asked (already set in the config)
caveats: Adding a handle to allowFrom also puts it on the /approve approver list, and iMessage has no separate approver list. A plugin cannot check who resolved an approval (its onResolution callback receives only the decision), and the roadmap already records that 2026.9.7 cannot tie an approval to the person whose agent asked. What protects the parents is that the guest agent has no tools and so raises no approvals, and that prompts go only to the chat that asked, so a guest never sees an approval id. The roadmap's alternative for non-approvers, admission by pairing, costs a pairing-code reply to unknown numbers.
Most sitters will just text the parents. The realistic user is a grandparent who stays for days and writes in another language.

The guest must be on iMessage. A WeChat channel exists only as an external plugin maintained by Tencent's Weixin team with a QR login of a personal account; adding it for one relative is a much bigger change than this feature. WhatsApp is on the never-list.
The card goes to a cloud model and to a person outside the two-parent circle. Put on it only what you would tape to the fridge: no door codes, no Wi-Fi password, no policy or record numbers.
The install uses the allowlist policy, so strangers get silence. Under the pairing policy an unknown number would be sent a pairing code; do not switch to it for guests.
The relayed 'tell the parents' text is written by an outsider. Deliver it as a clearly quoted line; if it lands in a parent's agent session it is untrusted text sitting next to private memory.
safety: The guest agent has no tools and no memory, so the card is all there is to leak and it was written for that reader. It reads only the guest's own messages. Its only ways out are a reply to that guest and the verbatim relay to the two parents, which is done in code and not by the model. It is a shared agent and, by the roadmap rule, holds no accounts. It is never used for the children.
unverified: That allowFrom entries have no built-in expiry; none was found in the installed docs.
Whether the guest agent or the group agent would answer if a guest writes in a group chat with the parents.
Whether commands.allowFrom also governs /approve on iMessage, or only the channel approver list does.
Whether a relay sent through the family delivery is mirrored into the receiving parent's agent session.
Whether a guest admitted through an accessGroup entry, instead of a literal handle, counts as an approver.

name: Standing orders: a written charter per recurring job
description: Each recurring family job gets a short charter in the agent's AGENTS.md: what Happy may do without asking, when it runs, what needs a yes first, when to stop and ask, and what it must never do. Parents can read it and changes go through the config repo. New against the catalog: G003 registers the jobs, but nothing states their authority in one reviewable place.
example: Job message at 19:30: "Run the evening brief per standing orders." Parent text: "From now on don't text me about bins when I'm travelling" becomes a line under that program's What NOT to do at the next deploy.
how:
`## Program: ` sections (Authority, Trigger, Approval gate, Escalation, What NOT to do, plus an execute-verify-report rule) in templates/person/AGENTS.md, rendered per person by gen-family from the same family.json5 entries that drive the G003 job registry. Each automation message points at its program instead of repeating it. Isolated jobs must not use `--light-context`, which skips the bootstrap files. Held by each

-main, and by each reader agent for its own program.
caveats: A charter is prompt text, not enforcement. It survives compaction because AGENTS.md is re-injected, but an injected page can still argue with it; the hard limits stay in tool policy and hooks.
AGENTS.md shares a bootstrap budget (20,000 characters per file by default). Keep each program to about ten lines.
Sub-agents get AGENTS.md only, and scheduled runs do not get MEMORY.md, so anything a program needs must be in AGENTS.md, the job message, or a tool result.
The documented examples are business programs (posting content, restarting services, sending reports to stakeholders). Family programs are read-and-notify only; do not copy those authorities.
A chat instruction does not change the charter: config writes from chat are off and the agents have no file tools, so it waits for a deploy.
safety: Charters narrow behaviour and grant nothing. Never-list items are written under What NOT to do and are also unreachable by tool policy. No change to which agent holds private data, reads untrusted content, or can send.

name: Unattended-job guardrails (failure alerts, auto-disable, missed runs)
description: Rules that stop scheduled family jobs from failing silently or misfiring after an outage: failures alert Tony rather than the family, a job that keeps failing stops itself, stale runs are skipped after a power cut, and every job has a time limit and a tool cap. New against the catalog: the built-in scheduler behaviour and defaults that G003 and G008 should be built on.
example: The 19:30 brief fails twice in a row: Tony gets one text, and one more when it recovers. After a power cut, the 07:00 brief does not turn up at 11:40.
how: In happy-config: a global `cron.failureAlert` object routed to the operator's handle, so alerts do not fall back to each job's own announce target; `--timeout-seconds` and an explicit `--tools` cap on every job the G003 registry emits; `cron.skipMissedJobs: true` for recurring jobs; `cron.triggers.enabled: false`, set before any agent is given the `automations` tool and kept until F029 deliberately turns triggers back on. happy-inspect reads `openclaw automations list --all` to catch auto-disabled jobs. The healthchecks dead-man switch stays as the only signal for a Mac that is off. Gateway-level; no agent gains anything.
caveats: By default a failure alert goes to the failing job's own announce target, so Jordan would receive "job failed" texts for her jobs unless they are rerouted.
Alerts start after 2 failures in a row with a 1-hour cooldown; repeats with the same cause count as one incident and one recovery notice closes it.
A recurring job is switched off after 10 failures in a row and then disappears from the default job list.
Without a per-job timeout an isolated agent job is bounded only by a 60-minute watchdog.
Jobs run inside the gateway. After a reboot with FileVault locked nothing fires and nothing alerts, and by default the scheduler catches up on missed recurring runs later.
One-shot reminders still catch up after an outage even with skipMissedJobs set; a late reminder is sometimes worse than none.

Once

-main has the automations tool, the agent offers to turn a repeated request into a schedule and creates it enabled with an immediate test run. That is pleasant, but those jobs are not in the G003 registry, so the registry diff must tolerate or report them.

Trigger scripts and script payloads run with the owning agent's full tool policy, exec included, in the Code Mode executor, and the docs name `cron.triggers.enabled` as their only switch. With triggers on, the `automations` tool also offers the model script payloads, trigger scripts and stream commands. Set `cron.triggers.enabled: false` before any agent is given that tool (F007, AUT-01, AUT-03). This switches off the trigger-script design of F029 until triggers are deliberately turned back on.
safety: Purely restrictive. Alert text shown in chat is a normalized cause (raw errors stay in run history), and routing alerts to the operator keeps one person's job details out of another person's thread.
unverified: The exact shape of the global `cron.failureAlert` object beyond the documented destination fields; validate in staging.
Whether scheduler-sent failure alerts pass through the G009 recipient-pin hook or bypass it.

Where the auto-disable notice lands. The docs say the owning agent receives it and that it stays active even when failure alerts are off, so it may reach the family member's thread instead of the operator's.

name: When the model is down: an honest failure, a same-vendor fallback, and jobs that need no model
description: With one cloud vendor and no local model, a provider incident makes Happy answer with a raw error or not at all. This sets what the family sees and what keeps working: one plain 'the model is down' line, an optional sibling-model fallback, and the alerts that never needed a model.
example: Trigger: gpt-6-sol returns server errors for ten minutes at 07:00 while the morning brief is due.
how:
Fact on this install: each person agent is generated with model.fallbacks: [], and the docs say an agent's primary is strict unless its model object lists fallbacks. So after the built-in retries any failure is surfaced as a terminal error that keeps the provider's HTTP status. Options, cheapest first. (1) Add gpt-6-luna on the same per-person provider id as the single fallback for

-main: one line in gen-family, since both models are already in that agent's modelPolicy.allow under the same key and store setting. This covers model-scoped incidents and rate limits, not a vendor-wide outage. The docs say a fallback is used for that turn only and a one-line notice is shown in direct chats. Mail and kid agents keep fallbacks: [] as the roadmap requires. (2) No cross-vendor fallback: it needs a second vendor's key and a new privacy decision, and the local route is the skipped M2. (3) Keep the important alerts model-free: the weather watch (F018) is specified as a --command-argv job and the kill phrase (G005) is a before_dispatch claim, so both work through an outage. Timed reminders (F007) and the morning brief are '--message' jobs, which the docs define as model-backed agent turns, so they fail with the model; a fixed-text reminder that must not be missed, such as bin day, has to be created as a command job that prints its line. A scheduled agent turn can also carry its own '--fallbacks' list. (4) Extend the health watch (G008): when the existing error-ratio alert has fired for N minutes, a host script sends each parent one fixed line and later one 'back' line by a model-free send: 'openclaw message send' to the pinned family handles, or a command job with announce delivery. The catalog's usual host path, 'openclaw agent --deliver', runs an agent turn and so cannot announce a model outage. 'openclaw models status --check' is not the detector: its own docs say a clean exit does not prove a request will succeed.
depends_on: decision: let the smaller sibling model answer when the main one fails
G008 health watch and the O1 error-ratio alert
caveats: OpenAI's status history listed 39 incidents in September 2026 and 23 in the first ten days of October across all its products. Most do not touch the API models Happy uses, but some did, for example 'elevated error rates across API models' on 17 Sep.
An answer from the smaller model can be worse than the usual one; the fallback notice tells the parent which model answered.
An API key that hits its monthly cap looks like an outage until the month ends; the fixed line should say 'limit reached' when that is the cause.
If the Mac, the home internet or iMessage is what failed, nothing here helps. The dead-man alert is then the only signal and it goes to Tony.
A scheduled brief that fails is simply missed unless the job's retry settings say otherwise.
safety: No new data path. The fallback uses the same provider id, key and store:false setting, and the notice is a fixed string to pinned family recipients. Mail and kid agents stay strict, so their content can never move to another model by accident.
unverified: The exact text a parent sees on iMessage when every candidate fails; the docs describe it, it was not triggered in this run.
Whether gpt-6-luna stays healthy during typical gpt-6-sol incidents.
Whether command jobs deliver normally while model calls are failing; nothing suggests otherwise but it was not tested.

How the hook learns which job produced a text; no doc lists a job id on message_sending, so the job may have to write its own tag into the text.

name: Nightly backups and a quarterly restore drill
description: Happy's memory, settings and history are copied every night to an encrypted place off the Mac's main disk, and a quarterly test proves the copy restores.
how: openclaw backup create --verify nightly via launchd or a command automation, encrypted with age; openclaw backup restore --target for the drill; separate tar for home-store and family.json5.
corrections: 'backup sqlite create --repository' alone is not a valid call and is not Git-versioned: it needs exactly one source (--global or --agent <id>) and writes plain snapshot directories. Git history is the separate 'openclaw backup git' command family.

Scheduling is not wholly outside the tool: 'openclaw backup enable --repository <dir> --every 24h' creates a nightly Git backup job. Only the archive and plain SQLite snapshot routes leave scheduling, rotation and encryption to the operator.

Secrets are not excluded by default (9 Oct 'needs' said they stay in Keychain): the full archive covers auth profiles and channel/provider credentials; only resolved secrets in the config copy are left out, and a secrets-excluding switch exists only for Git backups.
unverified: Whether a later memory-wiki vault is picked up as a plugin-declared backup resource or needs its own tar step.
The quarterly canary (answering a question from the restored copy) has no documented one-command path; activating restored state is an offline operator step.
Where the age key lives and whether the happy user can read it during a drill.

name: Local classifier calls (decision_evaluate with an on-device ONNX model)
description: A way to ask a small on-device model a yes/no, pick-one or score question (is this email urgent, does this text look like a bank statement, is this reply fine for an eight-year-old) and get a typed answer with a probability, with no cloud call. It is the missing piece behind the catalog's privacy gate, urgent-mail gate and kids classifier, and it does not depend on the skipped local-LLM milestone.
example: Trigger: the school-mail reader's hook asks one Boolean question about a new email's subject and first lines; only a probability above the threshold reaches the URGENT path.
how:
Release 2026.9.7 adds the decisionModel role and the core decision_evaluate tool, and plugins can call the same runtime from a hook through api.runtime.decisions.evaluate. The local provider is the @openclaw/onnx plugin, installed pinned to the Gateway version (npm:@openclaw/onnx@2026.9.7): zero-shot classifier presets on CPU in a separate worker process, with models fetched only by an explicit download command and checked against fixed hashes. Config is agents.defaults.decisionModel (or per agent) plus plugins.entries.onnx. Call it from the in-house hooks (F084 gate, F055 reader, later the F072 kids filters) rather than granting the tool to

-main.
depends_on: OpenClaw upgraded to 2026.10.1 or later (the published plugin declares that as its minimum)
A small labelled test set per question, so false positives and misses are measured before a gate relies on it
The co-versioned plugin release pinned at install (npm:@openclaw/onnx@2026.9.7), proven to load and pass its probe command on a test profile before any gate relies on it
caveats: The installed 2026.9.7 docs call the ONNX and TypeSafe plugins unpublished candidates; the npm registry shows @openclaw/onnx published at version 2026.10.1 with openclaw 2026.10.1 or later as a peer requirement, so it cannot be relied on with today's pinned Gateway.
These are generic zero-shot classifiers, not child-safety models; they can score and shortlist, but a kids deployment still needs its own evaluation and a second gate.
There is no fallback to the chat model when the decision provider is unavailable, and an unavailable result is not a 'no', so every gate has to fail closed.
The other provider, TypeSafe's hosted model, is a cloud service and out of scope.
Apple Foundation Models (F086) remain the alternative free on-device classifier.

The installed 2026.9.7 docs still call the ONNX and TypeSafe plugins unpublished candidates, but the npm registry now lists @openclaw/onnx 2026.9.6 through 2026.10.1, each requiring the same-numbered openclaw or later. The 2026.9.7 build (published 30 Sep 2026) matches today's pinned Gateway; the latest tag (2026.10.1) does not, so the version must be pinned at install. The plugin is weeks old, so treat it as experimental.
Each encoded input, rubric included, must fit 512 tokens and longer input is rejected rather than truncated, so a gate has to send a subject and first lines, or chunk a document itself.
Returned probabilities are model estimates, not calibrated; thresholds have to come from the labelled test set.
safety: This strengthens the architecture: the decision runs locally and returns a typed value rather than prose, and the hook, not the model, applies the threshold; the docs say results do not grant permission to act. Hostile text can still shift a score, so a classifier is a filter in front of a hard rule, never the rule itself. No data leaves the Mac.
unverified: Whether @openclaw/onnx 2026.10.1 loads on a 2026.9.7 host; its metadata lists a minimum host of 2026.9.6 but a plugin API of 2026.10.1
Classifier accuracy on this family's school mail and on kids' questions
Memory and CPU use of the worker process
Whether @openclaw/onnx 2026.9.7 installs and loads cleanly on this 2026.9.7 host; the installed docs predate its publication and describe only a source-checkout route
Which host the model download command fetches weights from and which egress rule it needs
